publications.title: A Journey of Dialogue and Discovery: My Experience in India
publications.author: Nurbolat Toktamys
publications.description: In 2025, I had the privilege of visiting India as a delegate of the 3rd India Central Asia Youth Delegation Forum. For me, the journey was more than a diplomatic event or an international conference.
publications.content:
In 2025, I had the privilege of visiting India as a delegate of the 3rd India Central Asia Youth Delegation Forum. For me, the journey was more than a diplomatic event or an international conference. It was a deeply meaningful opportunity to experience a country that has long maintained historical, cultural, and intellectual ties with Central Asia.

As someone who grew up in Kazakhstan and now teaches chemistry at the Nazarbayev Intellectual School in Turkestan, I have always been interested in how countries collaborate through education, science, and youth engagement. The forum offered exactly that: a platform where young professionals from Central Asia could exchange ideas with Indian counterparts about regional cooperation, innovation, and cultural understanding.

From the moment I arrived, India left a strong impression on me. The scale, diversity, and energy of the country was remarkable. Cities moved at an intense rhythm, yet there was also a sense of openness and curiosity among the people I met. India felt both ancient and modern at the same time – a place where centuries-old traditions coexist with technological innovation and ambitious economic development.

A traditional Indian reception for the Central Asian Youth Delegation, March, 2025

The Youth Forum itself was organised at a very high level by New Delhi. The program included discussions with policymakers, scholars, and young leaders who shared perspectives on regional cooperation between India and Central Asia. These conversations highlighted the strategic importance of strengthening people-to-people connections and building cross-cultural connections. While governments can establish diplomatic frameworks, it is often students, researchers, and young professionals who build the real bridges between societies.

One of the most memorable aspects of the visit was interacting with fellow participants from different countries. Delegates from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan had the opportunity to share their views on regional development and cultural exchange. At the same time, Indian participants introduced us to the intellectual and cultural diversity of their country. These conversations were not limited to formal sessions. Some of the most valuable exchanges happened during informal discussions, shared meals, and cultural visits.

India’s cultural richness also left a lasting impression on me. Walking through historical landmarks and observing daily life offered insights that no book or lecture could fully convey. The architecture, art, and traditions reflected a long and complex history that has shaped the identity of the country. At the same time, I was struck by how strongly young Indians are engaging with global issues such as technology, entrepreneurship, and sustainable development.

Another aspect that impressed me was India’s commitment to education and knowledge exchange. As an educator myself, I was particularly interested in how universities, research institutions, and policy think tanks collaborate to support innovation and international dialogue. The forum demonstrated that India sees education and youth engagement as important tools of public diplomacy and regional cooperation.

At the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, India

For me, the visit also reinforced the historical connections between Central Asia and India, which are more than a millennium old. For centuries, trade routes, cultural exchange, and intellectual interaction linked the two regions. Today, these connections continue in new forms through academic partnerships, cultural initiatives, and youth forums such as the one I attended. It was inspiring to see how modern diplomacy is built upon these historical ties.

One of my main takeaways from the experience is the importance of dialogue and mutual understanding. When people from different countries meet and share their perspectives, stereotypes disappear, and genuine partnerships can emerge. International cooperation becomes more meaningful when it is supported by personal relationships and cultural awareness.

As a teacher, this experience also influenced how I think about education. I realised that preparing students for the future requires more than strong academic knowledge. It also requires global awareness, cultural openness, and the ability to collaborate with people from different backgrounds. Experiences like the India – Central Asia Youth Forum demonstrate the value of international engagement in shaping the next generation of leaders.

From a meeting with educationists and industry leaders

When I returned to Kazakhstan, I shared my experiences with colleagues and students. Many of them were curious to learn more about India – its culture, society, and opportunities for collaboration. This exchange of stories and perspectives is exactly how international understanding grows: through individual experiences that inspire broader curiosity and dialogue.

Looking back, my visit to India was not only a professional opportunity but also a personal journey of discovery. It allowed me to see a country that is vibrant, diverse, and forward-looking. More importantly, it reminded me that meaningful cooperation between regions begins with human connections.

Initiatives such as the India – Central Asia Youth Forum play an important role in strengthening these connections. By bringing together young people from different societies, they help build the foundations for long-term cooperation and goodwill.

I hope that exchanges between India and Central Asia will continue to grow in the coming years. The potential for collaboration in education, science, culture, and innovation is enormous. For young professionals like me, participating in such initiatives is both a privilege and a responsibility – to carry forward the spirit of dialogue and partnership that these forums represents.
publications.authorBio: Nurbolat Toktamys teaches chemistry at the Nazarbayev Intellectual School of Science and Mathematics in Turkestan, Kazakhstan. He mentors students in scientific research and actively promotes international youth dialogue, educational collaboration, and cultural exchange between Central Asia and the broader Eurasian region.

publications.title: Eurasia in India's Strategic Calculus
publications.author: Dr. Pravesh Kumar Gupta
publications.description: IERF serves as a vital enabler in a rapidly transforming Eurasia, driving evidence-based continental re-engagement to help India build enduring strategic depth.
publications.imageFootnote: A view of the Rashtrapati Bhawan, New Delhi, India
publications.content:
A view of the Rashtrapati Bhawan, New Delhi, India

Globally, Eurasia refers to the world's largest continuous landmass, combining Europe and Asia as a single supercontinent. The term originated in the 19th century as a geographical construct. Later, it was popularised by political geographers to describe the combined Europe-Asia landmass without artificial divisions like the Ural Mountains. In geopolitical discourse, it gained prominence through Halford Mackinder's Heartland theory in the early 20th century. Mackinder’s Heartland theory suggested that control of the Eurasian core (especially Central Asia) is pivotal to global dominance. In the post-Soviet era, this geopolitical reading of Eurasia has evolved. Russian thinkers like Alexander Dugin advocated it as Eurasianism and have framed it as a unique civilizational space blending Slavic, Turkic, and steppe elements.

Because of the geostrategic location and abundance of natural resources, Eurasia has long been a playground for major power play in the twenty-first century. For each major power engaged in Eurasia, distinct conceptions of the construct reflect their geopolitical interests. Russia’s conception of ‘Sphere of Influence’ and resisting Western dominance in its backyard is one of its main geopolitical objectives in Eurasia. For China, the region is important for both economic and security interests. For the US and the West, Eurasia is seen as a theatre for containing Russia and China, the heartland’s dominant powers. While all such distinct national conceptions of Eurasia treat Central Asia as the locus region, the term itself has become a ‘definitional morass’, evading strict definitions or geographical strictures.

For India, Eurasia is not merely geographical but a civilizational and strategic continuum rooted in ancient linkages spanning across millennia. Much before the Silk Road, the Indian subcontinent, or South Asia today, frequently exchanged ideas, commodities, peoples and philosophies with this region. In the twenty-first century, it represents India's extended neighbourhood beyond the maritime domain, encompassing energy-rich Central Asia, the Caspian Sea linked-Caucasus region, and Russia. Afghanistan also occupies a pivotal place in India’s conception of Eurasia as it serves as an interface between Central and South Asia, and is sometimes treated simultaneously as part of India’s immediate and extended neighbourhoods.

Unlike the Western view of Eurasia as a heartland prize or Russian civilizational narrative, India's conception of Eurasia emphasises mutual respect for sovereignty, multipolarity, and balanced partnerships. The region itself is vital for India's energy security - oil, gas, uranium and critical minerals. The forces of extremism and radicalisation in the region, especially in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, makes the area of strategic interest to India. As a result, India has promoted counter-terrorism cooperation with Afghanistan and the Central Asian republic. Another major driving force in India’s Eurasia calculus include the imperative of trade diversification with this underexplored region, and to prevent its encirclement by any single power.

New Delhi's potential focus on the Eurasian region is also driven by its historical and cultural ties to Eurasian countries, especially Russia and the Central Asian Republics. For India’s Eurasia strategy, Central Asia serves as the core, Afghanistan as a gateway, the South Caucasus as a strategic partner for shared interests in regional connectivity, and Russia as a reliable partner. India rejects zero-sum games and aspires to forge strategic partnerships and alliances with countries with common interests in regional stability, economic development, and multilateral cooperation. India's view avoids ideological framing, focusing on developmental partnerships and is rooted in the principle of strategic autonomy.

New Delhi continues to describe the region as part of its ‘extended neighbourhood’ and a ‘natural partner.’ Yet, this narrative has not translated into tangible strategic or economic gains. The Eurasian region presents immense economic opportunities for India. By leveraging its historical connections with the region, India aims to foster stronger people-to-people relations, promote tourism, and enhance cultural diplomacy. Rich in natural resources and strategically located along key trade routes, the region offers the potential for enhanced trade, investment, and energy cooperation.

India can tap into these markets, diversify its economic engagements, and strengthen its energy security. India's engagement with Eurasia is also crucial for maintaining a balance of power in the region as it seeks to promote a multipolar Eurasian order as a precursor to a just multipolar world. Unlike China and Russia's increasing assertiveness in Eurasia through initiatives such as the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), India however, lacks strong institutional grounding or a regional grouping of its own through which it can actively participate in safeguarding its interests and counterbalance regional imbalances.

In the contemporary era, India's foreign policy has leaned towards the maritime domain (Indo-Pacific, Act East, Quad). On closer enquiry, this is partly due to the colonial legacy of the partition of South Asia in 1947 and the subsequent Pakistani refusal to allow India passage to Afghanistan and Central Asia. These structural constraints have led to relative Indian neglect of continental Eurasia in the last seven decades, despite enduring civilizational ties and several material linkages predating the partition of the subcontinent. India’s ‘Connect Central Asia’ policy in 2012 marked a shift, but implementation lagged amid maritime priorities and continuing instability in Afghanistan.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to all the five Central Asian countries in 2015 signalled a high point in India’s regional outreach. However, high-level exchanges have since remained limited; the last state visit to India by a Central Asian leader was of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in 2018. Even though India-Central Asia relations matured in the last decade, beginning with the institutionalisation of dialogue at the foreign ministers’ level in 2019, the first India–Central Asia Summit convened virtually in 2022, and the SCO Summit under India’s presidency held in a virtual format in 2023, the absence of sustained, in-person high-level engagements has contributed to a perception that India’s engagement with Central Asia has lost momentum.

Broader geopolitical developments, including the fallout of the Russian-Ukrainian war, tensions in West Asia centring Iran, and shifting Eurasian connectivity dynamics, are reshaping the strategic calculations of the regional countries in Eurasia. Regional states are increasingly pursuing multi-vector foreign policies while expanding their engagement with a wide range of external partners. These developments, while presenting a complex geopolitical situation, are opening a sliver of opportunity for India. The country is well-placed as a neutral balancer with strong and resilient ties with Russia and Central Asian countries.

However, limited connectivity and the gap between policy formulation and implementation continue to hinder India’s Eurasia strategy. To bridge this gap, India must adopt a consolidated, multi-pronged continental strategy prioritising alternative connectivity; including exploring air and digital connectivity. Leveraging soft power, including expanding educational cooperation, promoting cultural connections, bolstering people-to-people contacts and capacity-building programmes must be given high priority. In the absence of direct connectivity, incentivised investments (especially by private sector and through global arms of Indian public sector undertakings), localisation of bilateral economic activities, and digital cooperation have huge potential to grow.

Integrating Eurasia into India's broader grand strategy by balancing its maritime and continental dimensions is essential for sustained, meaningful engagement in the region. Despite geopolitical, logistical, and infrastructural barriers, New Delhi can steadily expand its influence through consensual partnerships that prioritize mutual respect for sovereignty and shared prosperity. Reclaiming India’s continental thinking in terms of foreign and defence policy does not necessarily mean undermining its maritime priorities. It only needs a thorough, interest-based reassessment of India’s strategic alignments through a bold engagement with the region and an ability to think beyond the obvious.

Against this evolving backdrop, the India Eurasia Research Forum (IERF) stands uniquely positioned to bridge persistent gaps and accelerate sustained, high-impact engagement between India and Eurasian stakeholders. As a dedicated platform focused exclusively on India-Eurasia ties, unlike broader think tanks with diversified mandates, IERF delivers targeted, high-quality research and facilitates multi-stakeholder dialogues. It convenes Track 1.5 and Track 2 initiatives that bring together government officials, domain experts, civil society, academia, and private-sector actors to address priority domains. This will include Physical and digital connectivity (including INSTC optimization, Chabahar synergies, air/digital corridors, and emerging tech linkages), security and counter-terrorism cooperation, energy security and critical minerals, cultural and people-to-people ties (education, tourism, capacity-building, and heritage diplomacy) and multipolarity and balanced regional dynamics.

Through regular seminars, webinars, policy roundtables, and Track 1.5 exchanges, IERF will generate actionable outputs such as commentaries, policy briefs, articles, joint research publications, and facilitate bilateral/multilateral exchanges. These efforts amplify India's strategic voice in Eurasian discourse while ensuring reciprocal insights flow back to New Delhi. This will help foster mutual understanding and consensus-driven partnerships.

In a rapidly transforming Eurasia, marked by multi-vector foreign policies and connectivity realignments, IERF will serve as a vital enabler. By driving evidence-based continental re-engagement, it will help India build enduring strategic depth that complements its continental priorities, safeguarding national interests through sovereignty-respecting cooperation and shared prosperity.
publications.authorBio: Dr. Pravesh Kumar Gupta is an Associate Fellow at the Vivekananda International Foundation (VIF). He is also the Research Advisor to the India Eurasia Research Forum (IERF). Dr. Gupta is an expert on Eurasian geopolitics and his research focuses on the society and politics of Central Asia, energy security and sustainability, and trans-regional connectivity linkages between Central and South Asia.

publications.title: Kurultai: Understanding the political transformation in Kazakhstan
publications.author: Dr. Pravesh Kumar Gupta
publications.description: Kazakhstan’s first Kurultai election marks a significant step in the country’s ongoing political transformation. This article examines the shift to a unicameral legislature, the reforms under President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, and the debate over whether the new political architecture will deliver meaningful pluralism and oversight. It also explores the broader implications for Central Asia and Kazakhstan’s growing partnership with India.
publications.content:
Kazakhstan, the largest country in Central Asia by both landmass and economy, is in the middle of a political transformation. The political reform process, which began after the January 2022 protests, has culminated in constitutional amendments. These amendments passed in a nationwide referendum in March 2026, took effect on July 1, and paved the way for parliamentary elections. On August 23, 2026, Kazakhstan will hold its first Kurultai election. These elections are highly significant and are being observed by regional and international observers. These elections are more about testing a whole new political architecture than picking winners.

The constitutional amendments under President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev include abolishing the two-chamber parliament (the Mazhilis and Senate) in favour of a single 145-seat legislature (called Kurultai). The reasoning behind the decision to move from a bicameral parliament to a unicameral legislature is to shorten the law-making process and help legislation move faster. Elections will be conducted through closed party-list proportional voting across one nationwide constituency, with a 5% threshold and five-year terms. There is also a built-in quota: women, youth, and people with disabilities have to make up at least 30% of any party's candidate list, though in practice they are already clearing 40%.

Seven parties have registered for the polls. Notably absent is Amanat, the long-ruling party, which chose not to run and instead folded into a new formation called Adilet. The new party is led by Aibek Dadebay, who was the head of the presidential administration. The rest of the political parties, Auyl, Respublica, Aq Jol, the People's Party of Kazakhstan, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party, and Baytaq, bring the total candidate pool to around 545. There have been differing viewpoints in international media with regard to the ongoing political transformation in Kazakhstan. One recurring question remains: Is it true pluralism, or merely a refined version of the same managed system?

Even the nomenclature of the new parliament, "Kurultai", is a well-considered term that has been grabbing political attention. The term has been taken from the old Turkic-Mongol steppe assemblies, the councils that once settled questions of leadership, war, and resource distribution in the Kazakh Khanate. It also refers to the consultative National Kurultai that ran from 2022 to 2026, which was dissolved along with the old constitution. With this terminology, the reform presents itself as a revival of indigenous governance traditions rather than an import of Western parliamentary norms. The new political arrangement simplifies the machinery of government by scrapping the upper house and eliminating presidential appointment quotas.

The Kazakh President has claimed that these reforms are intended to make governance better and more convenient, but apprehensions remain. The worry is that a pure list system, paired with a narrower field of parties, funnels influence into fewer, more manageable channels. This could make the Kurultai as a smoother-running rubber stamp rather than a genuine check on the executive. Whether that apprehension holds or fades away will depen entirely on how this body actually behaves once it's seated, and that's the real test of President Tokayev's "listening" pitch.

Kazakhstan's political reconfiguration also has broader regional impact in Central Asia. Kazakhstan's size both economic and demographic makes it Central Asia's natural anchor, and probably the region's most committed practitioner of multi-vector diplomacy. A legislature that can actually turn international commitments into domestic law, plan multi- year energy and connectivity projects, and provide real oversight would give Astana more room to lead on things like C5 cooperation, transport corridors, water and climate policy, and critical minerals — all while balancing relationships with Russia, China, the West, and

Türkiye. If parliament becomes a genuine player, Kazakhstan's foreign policy starts looking less like it hinges on one man's preferences and more like something durable. Neighbors dealing with their own governance headaches will be watching closely. This could either cement Kazakhstan's reputation as a stable reform laboratory or become a cautionary tale about the limits of redesigning institutions from the top down.

There's a bilateral aspect also. India and Kazakhstan have built a steady partnership since the early 1990s. Kazakhstan has long been India's biggest trading partner in Central Asia spanning uranium and oil, critical minerals, pharma, digital tech, agriculture, and connectivity. With India chairing BRICS in 2026 and Kazakhstan on board as a partner country, plus ongoing CICA engagement, a functioning unicameral parliament opens up new channels for parliamentary diplomacy, legislative exchanges, and alignment on things like bilateral investment protection and mobility rules. That India sent observers to this election is itself a signal — both countries have a stake in seeing whether Kazakhstan's institutions can be trusted to deliver. A more predictable legislative partner in Astana would help both sides pursue what they each want from a multipolar Eurasia: diversified supply chains, energy routes that don't depend on any single power, and stronger regional connectivity that feeds into India's own outreach to Central Asia.

None of this amounts to a democratic breakthrough. It is a carefully crafted renovation, not a revolution. What actually matters isn't the vote itself but what comes after: whether this new legislature can build the muscle for real deliberation, oversight, and lasting policy work. Pull that off, and Kazakhstan strengthens its hand both regionally and as a partner for India. If the proposed changes are implemented suitably it will make Kurultai name remembered for its impact. If not then this will remain a symbolism rather than anything it actually accomplished. People in Kazakhstan are ready for change. Making the government efficient is a prerequisite for a modernised Kazakhstan.

publications.title: Russian literary traditions and the formation of Eurasianism
publications.author: Sujal Yadav
publications.description: While the term "Eurasia" originated as a geological label, "Eurasianism" was born in the 1920s not in the minds of geographers, but among exiled Russian linguists, literary critics, and philosophers. Through literary reviews and structural linguistics, intellectuals like Prince Nikolai Trubetskoy built a movement asserting that Russia is a wholly unique civilization—distinct from both Europe and Asia. By treating contemporary literature as a contested space, these founders laid the intellectual groundwork for a worldview that continues to shape modern Russian geopolitical identity.
publications.content:
The terms “Eurasia” and “Eurasianism” hold a distinct dual significance in contemporary discourse. Eurasia is a geographical term introduced by the Austrian geologist Eduard Suess in the 1880s, denotes the unified tectonic continent of Europe and Asia, as detailed by Mark Basin in his historical survey.In contrast, Eurasianism (евразийствo) emerged as an influential intellectual movement among Russian émigrés in the early 1920s, asserting that Russia constitutes a unique civilization, distinct from both Europe and Asia. Notably, this movement did not originate with geographers or geopoliticians, but rather with philologists, literary critics, philosophers, and poets whose intellectual frameworks were shaped by textual analysis. Consequently, examining the Russian literary tradition is crucial for understanding the development of Eurasianism.

A literary Movement 

The founding circle of classical Eurasianism consisted primarily of members of the late Imperial Russian cultural elite in exile. Key figures included the linguist Prince Nikolai Trubetskoy, a pioneer of structural phonology; economic geographer Petr Savitsky; theologian Georgy Florovsky; and music and art critic Petr Suvchinsky. Additional members such as historian George Vernadsky, philosopher Lev Karsavin, lawyer Nikolai Alekseev, and notably, literary scholar and critic Dmitry Svyatopolk-Mirsky, further shaped the movement. As Igor Torbakov observes in his essay for the Institute for Human Sciences, these individuals were “young men in their late 20s and early 30s, scions of imperial noble families, highly educated and fluent in multiple European languages,” who had “lost everything” and reimagined their homeland as a colonized nation. The movement’s leadership by linguists and critics naturally led to the adoption of literary procedures and metaphors in constructing its worldview.

This orientation is evident in the movement’s publishing activities. In addition to theoretical works such as the 1921 Sofia manifesto Iskhod k Vostoku (“Exodus to the East”) and the periodical Evraziisky Vremennik, the Eurasianists published a literary review, the almanac Versty (“Milestones,” Paris, 1926–1928), edited by Suvchinsky, Svyatopolk-Mirsky, and Sergei Efron, with contributions from Marina Tsvetaeva and Lev Shestov. As A. A. Revyakina demonstrates in her comprehensive study of Eurasianist literature, Versty intentionally challenged émigré conventions by publishing Soviet poets and prose writers—Babel, Bely, Esenin, Pasternak, Selvinsky, Tynyanov—alongside Tsvetaeva, Rozanov, and Fedorov. The editors aimed to highlight “the most alive” elements in Russian literature, both pre-revolutionary and Soviet. Thus, the movement regarded contemporary literature as a contested space where the Eurasian thesis could be affirmed or refuted.

The Legacy: Slavophiles, Danilevsky, Leontiev

Eurasianism developed from a well-established literary and philosophical tradition rooted in nineteenth-century Russian literature. The Slavophiles Khomyakov, the Kireevsky brothers, and Aksakov argued that Peter the Great’s enforced Westernization disrupted Russia’s authentic national development. The Eurasianists adopted from Nikolai Danilevsky’s Russia and Europe (1869) the idea of unique, incommensurable “cultural-historical types,” and embraced the provocative notion of reducing Europe to a “peninsula of Asia.” They also drew on Konstantin Leontiev’s organicist and anti-egalitarian cultural perspective, as well as his emphasis on Russia’s connections with Turkic and “Turanian” peoples rather than Western Slavs. Revyakina identifies Leontiev, both a novelist and diplomat, as the movement’s “closest precursor” due to his consistent rejection of the West. These predecessors contributed both creative and critical works within political philosophy, which the Eurasianists integrated into their literary and intellectual heritage.

The movement’s title itself carried a poetic resonance. The Eurasianists adopted the epigraph “We are not the West, and not quite the East … we are the integral East” from émigré poetry. The central work of the 1921 anthology was Trubetskoy’s influential essay Europe and Mankind, which historian V. Ya. Pashchenko describes as “an intellectual insurrection against the absolutisation of a singular culture—the Romano-Germanic—associated with Europe.”

The intellectual uprising was carried out, characteristically, within the domain of cultural criticism. 

Trubetskoy and the Literary Argument for Civilizational Pluralism

Trubetskoy provides the most explicit example of literature shaping Eurasianist doctrine. As R. R. Vakhitov demonstrates in his analysis of Trubetskoy’s literary theory, Trubetskoy was not simply a political theorist with literary interests; he developed a systematic literary theory that directly reflected the core Eurasianist argument. Trubetskoy rejected the notion of a singular “world literature” hierarchically structured with European forms at the apex. Instead, he argued that each civilization possesses a unique and autonomous literary tradition, valuable on its own terms. Evaluating medieval Russian texts or the Russian folk chastushka by European literary standards, in his view, constituted a fundamental error and amounted to cultural colonization through aesthetics.

Trubetskoy’s formal analysis of Afanasy Nikitin’s fifteenth-century travelogue Journey Beyond Three Seas exemplifies this approach. By examining the text’s alternation between calm narrative and religious-lyrical digression, as well as Nikitin’s use of Arabic, Persian, and Turkic languages to express his most personal and religious sentiments, Trubetskoy demonstrated that “unadorned” Old Russian prose was constructed from sophisticated literary devices with distinct purposes. This literary-critical validation of non-European texts as possessing their own artistry parallels the geopolitical assertion that Russia-Eurasia constitutes a self-contained world that should not be evaluated by Western standards. Vakhitov observes that this methodology aligns with Trubetskoy’s structural approach in linguistics and Savitsky’s “Eurasian science” in geography, illustrating that the formal method in literature, the structural method in language, and mestorazvitie (“topogenesis”) in geography collectively represent a unified civilizational pluralism.

Formalism, the East, and the Reading of Russian Authors 

Eurasianist literary criticism extended beyond ideology to include substantive analyses of Russian authors, which in turn reinforced the movement’s theoretical framework. Trubetskoy maintained intellectual correspondence with Roman Jakobson, and the movement was closely aligned with Russian Formalism, particularly the OPOYAZ school’s emphasis, as Jakobson stated, on studying “literariness” rather than literature itself. However, the Eurasianists repurposed Formalism for civilizational aims: form was not an end in itself, but a means of expressing the spirit of a national literature at a specific historical moment, as Vakhitov emphasizes. Svyatopolk-Mirsky regarded the seventeenth-century autobiography of Archpriest Avvakum as a lost foundation for a distinct Muscovite literary language, while Suvchinsky interpreted Leskov, Blok, and Dostoevsky through the lens of “creative will” and “the Russian elemental force” (русская стихия). Blok’s works, such as On the Field of Kulikovo and The Scythians, with their imagery of the steppe and orientation toward the East, were repeatedly cited as artistic validations of the Eurasian belief that “Asia” was intrinsic to the Russian national spirit.

Dostoevsky occupied a distinctive position within Eurasianist thought. The Eurasianists and their supporters, including American scholar Clarence Manning in his 1925 study Dostoevsky and Scythism, viewed Dostoevsky as the foremost imaginative witness to Russia’s function as a “mediator” and “link” between East and West. He was seen as a writer who distanced himself from both the Westernizers, who positioned Russia as subordinate to Europe, and the Slavophiles, who simply opposed Europe. In this framework, Dostoevsky’s work was not merely illustrative but served as substantive evidence for the theory, providing a body of testimony regarding national character that could be utilized by geographers and historians as factual support.


The Neo-Eurasian Now: Gumilev and the Émigré Almanac 

By the late 1930s, classical Eurasianism had largely ceased to exist as an organized movement, persisting primarily through the solitary efforts of Savitsky. Its subsequent revival is largely attributed to historian and ethnologist Lev Gumilev (1912–1992), son of poets Nikolai Gumilev and Anna Akhmatova. As Hildegard Kochanek notes in her critical study of his theory of ethnogenesis, Gumilev’s literary heritage conferred significant moral authority in Russia. Gumilev corresponded with Savitsky from 1956 and explicitly identified himself as “the last of the Eurasianists.” His speculative theory of passionarnost’ (“passionarity”), which posits bursts of bio-cosmic energy as drivers of the rise and fall of ethnoi, reframed civilizational pluralism in pseudo-scientific terms. However, as Kochanek argues, its emotional resonance derived from a fatalistic, mythic narrative of perpetual conflict between Russian-Eurasian and Western “super-ethnoi.” New Lines Magazine characterizes Gumilev’s historical writing as “fantasy, poetry and plain pseudo-history,” underscoring the blurred boundary in this tradition between literary creation and ideological dogma.

The intellectual trajectory extends from Gumilev to the post-Soviet 'neo-Eurasianism' of Aleksandr Dugin, who reinterpreted—and, according to critics, frequently distorted the classical tradition into an expansionist geopolitical doctrine. This evolution is also reflected in the official rhetoric of a distinct 'Eurasian civilization' associated with the Eurasian The intellectual trajectory extends from Gumilev to the post-Soviet neo-Eurasianism of Aleksandr Dugin, who successfully adapted the classical tradition into a comprehensive geopolitical doctrine advocating a multipolar world. This evolution is also reflected in the official rhetoric of a distinct 'Eurasian civilization' associated with the Eurasian Economic Union and Russian state ideology since the early 2000s. Scholars recognize that the doctrine’s persistence is largely attributed to its inherent adaptability and capacity to foster regional integration . Despite these transformations, the core literary-critical principle endures: the rejection of a universal standard and the affirmation that each civilization possesses its own “cultural code,” a concept rooted in Trubetskoy’s assertion that every literature should be interpreted according to its own criteria.

The Paradox, and What It Means Today

The central paradox of Eurasianism is particularly evident in its literary foundations. The movement developed a robust anti-colonial discourse, anticipating Edward Said by several decades, by linking imperial authority to disciplinary knowledge and aesthetic judgment. Simultaneously, it maintained an implicit imperial agenda, reimagining the Romanov and Soviet territories as an “organic” Eurasian entity. The same literary nationalism that challenged European condescension toward medieval Russian prose and folk traditions could, in Gumilev’s theory and subsequent neo-Eurasian rhetoric, be redirected toward xenophobia and the rejection of “universal human values.” Examination of the literary sources reveals that Eurasianism functioned not merely as a geopolitical concept, but as a distinctive interpretive approach to the steppe, the nation, and the Russian literary canon.

This constitutes the principal insight for contemporary discourse . Eurasia and Eurasianism, whether considered as meta-geographical constructs, geopolitical strategies, or civilizational identities, cannot be adequately understood through geography or international relations alone. Their foundational logic was established by literary figures who, following Trubetskoy, maintained that the essence of a people is most authentically revealed in its literary forms. The Russian literary tradition did not simply parallel the development of Eurasianism; it provided its methodology, metaphors, and much of its evidentiary basis. Thus, to study one is inherently to study the other.
publications.authorBio: Sujal Yadav is a Senior Research Scholar at the Centre for Russian and Central Asian Studies, SIS, JNU, and the Co-founder, Deputy Director of the India Eurasia Research Forum, an academic platform dedicated to fostering research, scholarly exchange, and dialogue on contemporary Eurasian affairs. His research focuses on Russian cultural diplomacy, Eurasian studies, and India–Russia relations, with particular interest in Russia’s engagement with the wider Eurasian region. He also serves as a Guest Lecturer in Russian Language and Culture at the Department of Slavonic and Finno-Ugrian Studies, University of Delhi.
